newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Cardoso says he wants faster land reform.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Cardoso says he wants faster land reform.

text.p: President Fernando Henrique Cardoso said on Friday he wanted to speed up land reforms, a day after landless peasants marched to the Brazilian capital in the biggest demonstration in recent years.
About 1,500 members of the Landless Movement (MST) marched 750 miles (1,200 kms) to Brasilia where they were joined on Thursday by some 25,000 people protesting Cardoso's policies.
"The MST has my support. I am in favour of agrarian reform. I will receive the MST," Cardoso told national CBN radio.
Cardoso was due to meet later on Friday with leaders of the MST, a new left-wing force that has made land ownership, concentrated in the hands of few Brazilians, a major issue.

Crowds of protestors waving red flags brought Brasilia to a standstill on Thursday, recalling the massive protests that helped topple President Fernando Collor in December 1992 amid a corruption scandal.
Many of the MST marchers remained camped in tents near the presidential palace on Friday waiting to take part in another demonstration over land and labour rights on May 1.

Cardoso acknowledged the impact Thursday's demonstration had on Brazilian public opinion: "It could prove a turning point for society because it can now see the problems that exist in the countryside."
The president said his target of settling 280,000 families in four years compared favourably with a total of 218,000 families settled in the 20 years before he took office.

Cardoso also said he understood why landless families fed up with political delays chose to invade unused farmland. But he urged the MST to halt its campaign of occupations that have led to clashes with police and farm guards.
"We can do more...but only if the MST, instead of invading land and undermining negotiations, adopts a more open attitude. Then we can make progress," the president said.

More than 100 people have died in clashes over land since Cardoso took office in January 1995. The MST says it will step up land occupations to keep up pressure on the government to settle up to one million families over the next two years.
Brazil has one of the world's most unfair land distribution ratios with about half of the arable land in the hands of just two percent of the country's landowners.

Officials said there was not much more they could do to speed up land reform. Merely turning over land to the landless without the necessary credit and technical support would condemn settlers to never-ending poverty, they said.

"When people say the solution for land reform is the settling of one million families, we're talking about a cost of $40 billion," said presidential spokesman Sergio Amaral, adding that taxpayers might balk at having to foot the bill.
